title: Given a string, find the minimum number of character deletions needed to make it a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence DP pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Minimum Deletions to Make a String Palindrome (Fewest Removals for Symmetry)

s1_definition.profdef: The Minimum Deletions to Make a Palindrome problem is solved through the Palindromic Subsequence pattern. The characters we must keep form the longest palindromic subsequence, so the characters we must delete are everything else, which means the answer is the string length minus the length of the longest palindromic subsequence. That gives a quadratic time and space dynamic program.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to normalise certain legacy account tags into a symmetric canonical form and asks how many characters must be removed to make a given tag read the same both ways. The fewest deletions equal the length of the tag minus its longest symmetric core.
s1_definition.oneliner: Minimum deletions equal the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Minimum Deletions to Make a Palindrome problem is solved through the Palindromic Subsequence pattern. The characters we must keep form the longest palindromic subsequence, so the characters we must delete are everything else, which means the answer is the string length minus the length of the longest palindromic subsequence. That gives a quadratic time and space dynamic program.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to normalise certain legacy account tags into a symmetric canonical form and asks how many characters must be removed to make a given tag read the same both ways. The fewest deletions equal the length of the tag minus its longest symmetric core.

**One line to remember:** Minimum deletions equal the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.

sections.s2_technical:
The characters that stay must themselves form a palindrome and must keep their original order, which is exactly the definition of a palindromic subsequence. To delete as few as possible we keep as many as possible, so we keep the longest palindromic subsequence and delete the rest. Therefore the answer is the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.

We compute the longest palindromic subsequence with the two-ended range table: `for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) { dp[i][i] = 1; for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) dp[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j) ? 2 + dp[i+1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]); }` and then return `n - dp[0][n-1]`. A concrete check: for a tag of length six whose longest symmetric core is four, two deletions are required. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, the same number equals the minimum insertions to make a palindrome because inserting a mirror character is symmetric to deleting an unmatched one, and both reduce to the same longest palindromic subsequence quantity.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is normalising legacy account tags into a symmetric canonical form during a data migration, and it needs to know, for each tag, the fewest characters it must remove to make the tag read the same forward and backward. Trying all deletion combinations is exponential. This is exactly how the Minimum Deletions to Make a Palindrome works: it computes the longest symmetric core with the Palindromic Subsequence pattern and subtracts it from the length.

The code defines a `TagNormalizeService` exposing `minDeletions(tag)` returning the minimum deletions. A `Demo` runs it over a sample tag and logs the deletion count.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the tag ABCDBA. We want the fewest deletions that make it a palindrome.

Step 1 — We build the longest palindromic subsequence table. Single characters seed the diagonal with length one.

Step 2 — The ends A and A of the whole tag match, so the answer for the full range is two plus the core of the inner range BCDB.

Step 3 — Inside BCDB the ends B and B match, giving two plus the core of CD. The ends C and D of CD differ, so its core is the larger of the two singles, which is one. So BCDB has core three.

Step 4 — The full range therefore has longest palindromic subsequence two plus three equals five, meaning ABABA style core ABDBA of length five sits inside the six-character tag.

Step 5 — The minimum deletions equal six minus five, which is one, since removing the single unmatched character leaves a palindrome. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:12:04 PM com.bank.tagnorm.service.TagNormalizeService minDeletions
INFO: Min deletions to make ABCDBA a palindrome = 1
Oct 27, 2026 9:12:04 PM com.bank.tagnorm.TagNormalizeApplication main
INFO: Deletions to canonicalise tag ABCDBA is 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: tag = "ABCDBA" (length 6)
    │
    ▼
  longest palindromic subsequence table
    │ ends A==A → 2 + core(BCDB)
    │ BCDB: B==B → 2 + core(CD)=1 → 3
    │ full range → 2 + 3 = 5
    ▼
  answer = length - LPS = 6 - 5 = 1
    ▼
  Output: min deletions = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Minimum Deletions to Make a Palindrome reduces cleanly to the Palindromic Subsequence pattern once I notice that the characters I choose to keep must already form a palindrome in their original order, which is precisely a palindromic subsequence. To delete as few characters as possible I keep as many as possible, so I keep the longest palindromic subsequence and the answer is simply the string length minus that length.

I compute the longest palindromic subsequence with the standard two-ended range table, matching the two ends to add two to the inner answer and otherwise dropping one end, and then I subtract the corner value from the length. This stays in quadratic time and space. A point I always make is that this exact same number is also the minimum insertions needed to make the string a palindrome, because inserting a mirror of an unmatched character is the symmetric operation to deleting it, and both reduce to the same longest palindromic subsequence quantity.

At the National Bank of India I used this during a data migration that normalised legacy account tags into a symmetric canonical form, where the team needed the fewest characters to remove to make each tag read the same both ways. I computed the longest symmetric core and subtracted it from the tag length. Explaining that the kept characters are a palindromic subsequence, that the deletions are the leftover characters, and that the same figure doubles as the minimum insertions is what demonstrates to an interviewer that I understand this application of the Palindromic Subsequence pattern.
